Yes. 

The story convincingly explores the perspectives of two characters who act in flawed, unappealing ways, yet makes their motivations deeply believable and human. 

First, the narrator acts in a way many would find objectionable: out of petty jealousy and insecurity, he completely ghosts his best friend—a person who had only ever shown him exceptional kindness—when asked to be in his wedding. However, the writer presents the narrator's mindset with such psychological accuracy ("Admiration, over time, curdles into a low and private annoyance, like a tooth") that his actions feel entirely consistent and understandable, rather than simply villainous.

Second, we see the perspective of Q (Quentin) in his adulthood, behaving in a cowardly, evasive manner toward a colleague he has removed from a project. Through his dialogue and body language, the story captures the specific moral failure of someone who is so attached to being perceived as "good" and kind that he ends up being cruel through avoidance. Watching Q break down ("I'm not very good at this part. I know people think I am") transforms him from an idealized figure into a complex, three-dimensional character, and the inclusion of Marianne's sharp, dignified perspective further enriches the scene.
